new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls predominantly on the penultimate syllable (79.6% of 1363 stress-marked tokens in Li's 1927 notecards; two-syllable words 84.5% initial, three-syllable 82.6% second, four-syllable 74.5% third, five-syllable 68.4% fourth). Li's older rule (stress on the stem if heavy, on the syllable before the stem if light) is treated as penultimate stress with a deleted word-final enclitic. No lexical tone; Wailaki has a stress system.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described as such; about 1.5% of tokens are 'double marked' (two accent marks, on two prefixes or a prefix and the stem) and are left unexplained.
new_statements.exceptions: About 20% of tokens carry stress outside the penult; the conditioning factors (syllable weight, weight hierarchy, noun vs. verb) are explicitly left for further research. Phonetic correlates unknown since no recordings exist.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, based entirely on philological analysis of accent marks in Fang-Kuei Li's 1927 field notecards (431 cards, mostly verb paradigms and wordlist forms), i.e. citation/elicited forms of a dormant language; no acoustic data.
new_statements.identity_note: Begay 2018 uses 'Wailaki' as a cover term for the whole Eel River Athabaskan dialect continuum (Glottolog wail1244, ISO wlk; Golla 2011's Eel River Athabaskan, incl. Wailaki proper, Lassik, Nongatl, Sinkyone); the stress analysis rests on Li's 1927 data from Round Valley speakers (Wailaki proper). Cahto/Kato is a separate language and is not covered.

sources.note: Section 2.7 'Stress' (pp. 66-68): no audio exists; analysis of accent marks in Li Fang-Kuei's 1927 notecards (1363 stress-marked tokens) shows a clear preference for penultimate stress (79.6% overall; >=65% for every word length); Li's heavy/light stem rule (stress on stem if heavy, on syllable before stem if light) is reconciled with penultimacy via a deleted enclitic; no lexical tone; factors for non-penultimate placement (weight, word class) left open.
